title: The enforcement discretion
paras: Let's start with the enforcement discretion. Section 172 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 empowers an authority to issue an enforcement notice where it appears there's been a breach and it's expedient to issue one, having regard to the development plan and other material considerations — but notice it empowers, it never obliges. The N-P-P-F asks authorities to act proportionately when they respond to a suspected breach. Now, expedient doesn't mean convenient, politically comfortable, or popular with the complainant. It means the action serves a legitimate planning purpose, the harm justifies the resource, and what you're after is achievable and proportionate. So before you do anything, apply the public interest test: what planning harm is this breach actually causing, and does that harm justify action? The system was never designed to punish the absence of a piece of paper.

Sometimes not acting is exactly the right call — and it takes more confidence than serving a notice does. Take the marginal extension that's well designed, harms nobody and would be granted on application: that should draw a letter inviting a retrospective application. And if none comes and there's no material harm, you record a judgment that action isn't expedient, and you close the file. But the discretion isn't cover for inaction. Unauthorised works to a listed building, a felled protected tree, real harm to Green Belt openness, the commercial use generating continuous disturbance — these demand prompt action. The officer who spends six months negotiating while the breach beds in isn't exercising discretion. They're letting a problem get worse.

Negotiation resolves most breaches, but only if you're disciplined about it: a clear objective, a defined timetable, and the willingness to walk away when it stops producing progress. A deadline you don't enforce isn't a deadline. The developer who watches a stated date slide past with no consequence has learned that the authority's options apparently include doing nothing. So say what you expect and by when, make the timetable realistic for what you're asking, and mean it. And here's a distinction worth holding onto — the householder who genuinely didn't know, versus the developer running the clock on a twice-refused site. That's what decides which conversation to have.

However you exercise the discretion, record it — clearly, specifically, in terms a stranger could follow two years on. A decision not to act should set out the breach, the harm or its absence, the policy position, the representations, and why action isn't expedient. "No action — not expedient" defends nothing once the complainant reaches the ombudsman, who's looking at process, communication and transparency, not the planning merits. Consistency matters as well. Decline to act on one extension and you've created a practical precedent, so the officer taking a different view on the next one needs a recorded reason why the cases differ. A clear enforcement policy, and a prioritisation framework — high, medium, low, with defined response times you actually apply — that's what makes like cases alike.

title: Breach, immunity & evidence
paras: Now, breach, immunity and evidence. Section 171A defines a breach as development without the required permission, or failure to comply with a condition or limitation. Neither is a criminal offence. Mainstream enforcement is a discretionary civil regime, and the officer who treats the landowner as a suspect and the site as a crime scene has misunderstood the job. But the exceptions matter every bit as much as the rule. Unauthorised works to a listed building are a crime from the moment they're carried out — that's section 9 of the Listed Buildings Act: no notice needed, no time limit, penalties unlimited, and the harm often irreversible. Display an advertisement without consent and you've got an offence with a continuing daily element. Works to a tree protected by a tree preservation order are an absolute offence under section 210 — ignorance of the order is no defence. And removing a protected countryside hedgerow without notification under the Hedgerows Regulations 1997 is an offence — one that catches Class Q conversions out regularly. So categorise it civil or criminal first, because that defines the tools, the tone and the procedure.

Before you reach for any tool, establish there's a breach at all. Check the General Permitted Development Order — the G-P-D-O — before anything else. If the extension is permitted development, the investigation is over, and pressing on against permitted development is an embarrassing and expensive retreat. Internal works, maintenance, changes within a use class, de minimis matters, agricultural use of land — none of that is development, however many complaints land on your desk. On a material change of use, identify the planning unit correctly before you do anything — a farm may be one unit or several, and the wrong unit gives you a notice alleging the wrong breach on the wrong land. And keep lawfulness distinct from permission. A use that's immune through the passage of time is lawful by immunity, not approved. A certificate of lawfulness of existing use or development — a CLEUD — confirms the enforcement window has closed, and nothing more.

The time limits changed fundamentally on the 25th of April 2024. Section 115 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 replaced the four-year rule, so every breach occurring on or after that date now carries a single ten-year period. The transitional provisions leave us with a dual-track regime for years to come. Operational development substantially completed before the 25th of April 2024, and changes of use to a single dwellinghouse occurring before that date, keep the four-year limit — and misapply the split and you lose the case on ground D, with no remedy at appeal. Substantial completion means capable of use for its intended purpose, not fully finished — so the clock can be running while ancillary works are deliberately dragged out. Deliberate concealment — positive steps to hide the breach, not just a failure to advertise it — can disapply the limits through a Planning Enforcement Order from the magistrates, within six months of sufficient knowledge, and that gives you an enforcement year. And the second-bite provision, section 171B(4)(b), lets you take further action within four years of previous enforcement action where a notice turned out defective. That's a safety net, not a habit.

Investigation starts at a desk, not on a doorstep. Planning history, conditions, previous enforcement, land registry — so you serve the right people — aerial imagery and historic mapping, where the photographs showing bare land in 2019 defeat the claim of fifteen years' use, and the policy constraints that shape the expediency judgment. Then on site: systematic date-stamped photographs stored on authority systems, laser measurements rather than estimates, contemporaneous signed notes, and a careful record of anything said voluntarily — the date works started, who did them, what was intended. And go beyond the obvious sources: building control records, licensing, environmental health, council tax and the electoral register — often the thing that decides which time limit applies — plus social media or review histories that date a use precisely. The case file is the product. Everything else — the notice, the appeal statement, the prosecution — is only ever as good as the file it's drawn from.

title: The Planning Contravention Notice
paras: Next, the planning contravention notice. The P-C-N — that's section 171C of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 — can be served on an owner, occupier, or person with an interest in or carrying out operations on land, where it appears a breach may have occurred. The threshold is deliberately low: may, not has, not probably has. It's an investigative tool for when you need more information, not a way of drawing conclusions in a case that's already made out. And it's discretionary. Nothing obliges you to serve one before enforcing, and where the breach is clear and delay would let the situation worsen or the clock run, going straight to a notice is entirely proper.

It requires the recipient to state what operations have been carried out, what the land is used for, and whether conditions have been complied with — and it can invite them to say how any suspected breach might be resolved. The recipient has 21 days. Failing to respond is a criminal offence under section 171D, and so is a false or misleading response. In practice, the sanction for silence is rarely invoked, and the calculating recipient sometimes answers minimally or not at all. In which case you take the investigation forward by other means. The P-C-N fills gaps — it isn't a gateway you have to pass through.

It's not available for suspected breaches of the listed building, conservation area, hazardous substances or tree regimes, which carry their own investigative powers — serve a P-C-N on a listed building case and you've covered no bases at all. Nor can it compel self-incrimination where the conduct could give rise to criminal liability. Where the case is criminal in character, the PACE framework governs, and the P-C-N route isn't appropriate. And unlike enforcement notices, stop notices and breach of condition notices, a P-C-N isn't entered in the enforcement register, isn't a land charge, and doesn't bind a purchaser — so if the land changes hands mid-investigation, think about a fresh notice on the new owner.

It does its best work in change of use cases where the nature or history of a use is unclear, in condition cases where you need to establish the extent of non-compliance, and in cases where ownership or responsibility is uncertain. It's least useful — sometimes counterproductive — against clearly visible, clearly unauthorised operational development, where all it does is alert the recipient and hand them three weeks to prepare. But remember a signed response is evidence. The landowner who gives the authority one commencement date in a P-C-N response, and a different one at appeal, has an inconsistency to explain to an inspector.

title: Enforcement notices: drafting to survive
paras: Now to enforcement notices, and drafting to survive. Section 172 requires both elements — a breach, and the expediency judgment — and the decision has to be properly authorised. Usually that's under delegated powers, on a report setting out the breach, the harm, the merits and the expediency reasons, with committee authorisation considered where the case is politically sensitive or finely balanced. Section 173 dictates the contents. The land — a plan on an Ordnance Survey base, site edged red, because a verbal description just invites argument about scope. The matters constituting the breach. The steps required, or the activities to cease. The reasons why action is expedient. And the effective date and compliance period. Get any element wrong and you've handed over a ground of appeal.

The breach description is where more notices fail than anywhere else. It has to be precise enough that the recipient knows exactly what's alleged. Accurate, in that it describes what actually happened. In plain English — a section 179 prosecution can fail if a court finds the notice incomprehensible to a lay person. And complete: in mixed-use cases, you have to identify all the uses on the land, because section 173(11) deems permission granted for whatever a complied-with notice leaves standing. Here's the worked trap. A notice alleging only the unauthorised vehicle-repair use, on a site whose residential use was also never authorised, may, on compliance, deem permission for the very residential use the authority would have refused. So identify everything on the site first, then decide deliberately what to allege and what to leave.

The requirements are governed by the Mansi principle: compliance must leave the land as it was before the breach — no better and, this is the critical bit, no worse. So work out what existed before the breach, what changed because of it, and require precisely that difference. A notice loose enough to catch pre-existing development over-enforces, and one requiring reinstatement beyond what the alleged breach logically demands does the same thing in reverse. Deliberate under-enforcement, under section 173(3), is legitimate — requiring removal of the offending storey rather than the whole building — provided the deemed-permission consequence for what remains is a considered, recorded choice, and never a drafting accident. And the requirements have to match the breach description exactly. A mismatch between the two is the commonest avoidable drafting failure there is.

Compliance periods are tested against what a reasonable person would need, not what the authority would prefer. Weeks for a small structure or a clean cessation. Months for substantial demolition or a business relocation. And stepped periods where a use has to stop quickly but removal can follow. Then service: on the owner, the occupier and anyone with a materially affected interest — known mortgagees included — not more than 28 days after issue, and not less than 28 days before the effective date, with the statutory explanatory note on appeal rights. Do the land registry search immediately before service, not from last year's planning history. And if an appeal is lodged before the effective date, the notice is suspended until it's determined — which is exactly why a technically robust notice, one that's unattractive to appeal on drafting grounds, saves you months.

title: Stop notices & urgent intervention
paras: Stop notices, and urgent intervention. The stop notice, under section 183, is an accelerant bolted onto an enforcement notice — it can't stand alone. It prohibits specified activity within as little as three days of service, or immediately, where special reasons — urgent environmental harm, irreversible heritage damage, public safety — are stated and served with it. It can't prohibit the use of a building as a dwellinghouse. Though it can prohibit use of land as a site for a residential caravan — a distinction that sits close to the human rights arguments in traveller cases. Contravene it and you've committed an offence carrying an unlimited fine, on summary conviction or on indictment, with the court required to have regard to the financial benefit accrued. And that provision matters, because the profit from carrying on often dwarfs any modest fine.

The compensation risk, under section 186, is real, but it's been overstated historically. Compensation arises where the enforcement notice is quashed on grounds other than the planning merits — a technical or legal failure — or is varied or withdrawn otherwise than on a grant of permission. Where an inspector quashes the notice by granting permission on a ground A appeal, compensation isn't automatically payable, and section 186(5) bars compensation for any activity that was, while the stop notice was in force, a breach of planning control. The authority that has its fundamentals right — a genuine breach, correct time limits, proper service — carries far less exposure than the old caution suggested. The real exposure comes from fundamental error: stopping activity that was never a breach, was immune, or was defectively served.

The temporary stop notice, under section 171E, is the more practical first response. It's freestanding — you need no prior enforcement notice — effective immediately on display, and, since the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act, from the 25th of April 2024, it lasts 56 days rather than 28. That turns it from a scramble into genuine breathing room to investigate and draft properly. There are limits, mind. It's prohibitory only — it can't require demolition or reinstatement. It can't prohibit use of a building as a dwellinghouse. Compensation, under section 171H, arises only in four situations — an existing permission complied with, permitted development, a subsequent lawful development certificate, or withdrawal otherwise than on a grant. And you can't serve a second temporary stop notice on the same activity without intervening enforcement action — so let a temporary stop notice expire without follow-through and you've forfeited the immediate-intervention route. Section 103 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act added the listed building temporary stop notice: where you suspect unauthorised works to a listed building, halting them for 56 days is now the first tool to reach for, because the harm is too often permanent to sit and wait.

Once the notices have been served, upheld and ignored, three escalations remain. First, prosecution under section 179 for non-compliance: an unlimited fine, on summary conviction or on indictment — the former £20,000 magistrates' cap was removed in March 2015, by LASPO 2012 and S-I 2015 number 664 — with financial benefit reflected in the penalty. And it's chargeable for successive periods, so the developer who carries on after conviction can be prosecuted again and again, until non-compliance costs more than compliance. Second, direct action under section 178: entering the land, carrying out the required steps, and recovering the costs. And third, the injunction under section 187B — the system's remedy of last resort in all but the most urgent cases — for persistent deliberate defiance, irreversible harm in progress, or breaches you can credibly see coming before they start. Its force is simple: breach an injunction and you're in contempt of court, and contempt carries imprisonment. Courts have generally not required undertakings in damages from authorities acting in the public interest — so advice that dismisses the route on that ground deserves some scepticism.

title: Enforcement appeals: the grounds
paras: Finally, enforcement appeals, and the grounds. Appeal lies under section 174 on seven grounds, and each one maps to a vulnerability the notice should have been drafted against. Ground A: permission ought to be granted. That's the planning merits ground, running as a retrospective application, with a fee that lapses the ground if it isn't paid — and the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act curtailed its availability from the 25th of April 2024, cutting down its use as a pure delaying tactic. Ground B: the matters alleged haven't occurred — a factual challenge the authority has to meet on the balance of probabilities, with the evidence the investigation gathered. Ground C: the matters don't constitute a breach — the legal-analysis challenge that exposes a flawed categorisation. And ground D: out of time — now dominated by the 25th of April 2024 transitional split, and unanswerable at appeal if you got the limits wrong.

Ground E: defective service — not automatically fatal, correctable where no injustice results, but serious where someone with a material interest was deprived of the chance to appeal. Ground F: the requirements exceed what's necessary — Mansi territory, where the inspector trims over-enforcement. And ground G: the compliance period is too short — the least contentious ground, readily granted, and rather telling about the care taken in drafting. Anyone with an interest in the land, or any relevant occupier, may appeal — served or not — which is exactly why investigating interests before you serve prevents surprises. The appeal has to be received before the notice takes effect. There's no discretion to accept a late enforcement appeal, and lodging suspends the notice, and the compliance clock, until it's determined.

There are three procedures. Written representations for the straightforward cases. Hearings where structured discussion helps. And inquiries for complex cases needing cross-examination — with the authority entitled to argue for the simpler procedure where the appellant has asked for more than the case warrants. The statement of case has to address every ground raised, not just the comfortable ones, backed by the file evidence. And the Inspectorate's timetable isn't optional. Late submission can get evidence excluded, and in serious cases of delay the inspector can quash the notice for procedural failure alone — an avoidable, and very public, humiliation. The inspector can dismiss, quash, correct misdescriptions where no injustice results, or vary the notice. But a notice so fundamentally defective that correcting it would produce a substantially different notice can't be saved.

Costs follow unreasonable behaviour, not the event — and they run both ways. Against the authority: a notice clearly unsustainable on the merits, grounds of resistance with no realistic prospect, late or inadequate evidence, allegations the evidence doesn't support. Against the appellant: unmeritorious grounds, failure to engage, unreasonable delay — and authorities should apply for costs where the conduct warrants it. Then, after the decision. If the appeal is dismissed, the compliance period runs from the decision date — so diarise it and monitor, because a dismissed appeal begins the compliance phase rather than ending the case. If the notice is quashed, decide promptly whether a fresh notice is possible, whether time has run, and whether the site has changed. And any challenge beyond the inspector lies only to the High Court, on a point of law, under section 289 — within 28 days.
